consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same primary identification: 'isles/coastlands' (Hebrew 'iyyim) is a prophetic metonym for the distant Gentile nations and the farthest reaches of the earth, who will hear of and receive God's salvation (Isa 41–42, 49, 51, 60; Ps 97; Gen 10:5). Secondary streams: Revelation's fleeing islands as elements of the world order shaken in judgment; literal geography/coastlands; Patmos as exile/isolation; and, listed as rare, an allegorical church-as-island-amid-the-sea-of-the-world reading.
book_summary: The book identifies the island as 'a set-apart people rising from the sea of nations, waiting for God's law and preserved while surrounding kingdoms fall' — i.e., God's separated people/remnant standing out of and against the sea of nations, with cross-reference to a Sea & Waters chapter where sea = nations.
consensus_core_identification: Islands/isles = the distant Gentile nations themselves, the remote peoples at the ends of the earth who will receive God's law and salvation.
book_core_identification: Islands = a set-apart (covenant/remnant) people distinct from the nations, rising out of the 'sea of nations,' awaiting God's law and preserved through judgment on surrounding kingdoms.
boundary_disagreement: The book keeps some of the same proof-texts (Isa 42:4; 51:5 'the isles shall wait for his law/upon me') but reassigns their referent: the ones waiting are not distant Gentiles but a separated people. It also reclassifies Rev 16:20 from destruction-of-islands-in-judgment to a preservation-amid-collapse motif, and reads Gen 10:5 against its plain 'isles of the Gentiles' sense.
material_contradiction: Consensus says the isles ARE the Gentile nations; the book says the island is a people set apart FROM the sea of nations. The same term cannot in the same passages denote both the mass of Gentile nations and a people distinguished from and preserved out of those nations. Accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus's central identification, even though 'waiting for God's law' is retained verbally.
rationale: The book's core replaces the consensus referent rather than narrowing it. The consensus's minimum core is 'distant Gentile nations/ends of the earth'; the book's is 'a set-apart people rising from the sea of nations.' These are opposed identifications built on an explicit sea=nations symbolism, under which the island is by definition NOT the nations. The book's reading closely resembles the rare alternative noted in Responses C and D (church/believing community as solid ground amid the sea of the world), so it is not NOVEL, but that alternative was flagged as rare and non-primary, so relative to the consensus core the relation is DIVERGENT with partial reclassification of shared proof-texts (Isa 42:4; 51:5) and of Rev 16:20.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the book preserves the 'waiting for God's law' motif and could be read as merely specifying WHICH people the isles represent (a faithful remnant among distant peoples), especially since Isa 11:11 (remnant recovered from the islands) and Job 22:30 KJV ('island of the innocent') give the preservation reading some textual footing. But Gen 10:5 explicitly calls them 'isles of the Gentiles' and Rev 16:20 has every island fleeing, not being preserved, so the printed citations cut both ways and the referent is genuinely replaced, not refined.
